subject: physics

items.q: Light from a distant galaxy is compared with light from the same element produced in a laboratory on Earth. What is observed about the light from the galaxy?
items.correct: Its wavelength has increased
items.misconception: Its wavelength has decreased
items.why: Students remember that a shift happens but not its direction, and the mental picture of something being stretched or squashed is easy to reverse when the wave diagram is not drawn. Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, so a shift towards the red end must be an increase in wavelength. The specification defines red-shift as an observed increase in wavelength.

items.q: The light from galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than the light from galaxy A. What can be concluded about galaxy B?
items.correct: It is further away than A and moving faster than A
items.misconception: It is closer to us than A and moving faster than A is
items.why: Speed feels like the direct cause of the shift, so distance is treated as an unrelated piece of information rather than as part of the same relationship. The specification ties the three together: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. A large red-shift therefore indicates both a high speed and a large distance.
items.random_wrong: It is a larger and brighter galaxy than galaxy A is

items.q: The light from most distant galaxies shows red-shift. What does this observation provide evidence for?
items.correct: That space itself (the universe) is expanding
items.misconception: That galaxies fly outwards through fixed space
items.why: The name Big Bang suggests a bomb going off in a room, and everyday explosions do throw fragments out through unchanging air. The specification states that the red-shift is evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding. The expansion is of space, not motion of objects through a fixed space, which is why every distant galaxy is observed to be receding.
items.random_wrong: That the Earth sits at the centre of everything

items.q: According to the Big Bang theory, how did the universe begin?
items.correct: From a very small region that was extremely hot and dense
items.misconception: As an explosion of matter into a huge space already present
items.why: The everyday meaning of explosion involves material bursting outwards into surrounding space, and diagrams that show a bright point on a black background reinforce the idea of a pre-existing emptiness. The specification says only that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense. The red-shift evidence is that space itself is expanding, so space is part of what the theory describes, not a container the universe was placed in.
items.random_wrong: From a very large region that was extremely cold and sparse

items.q: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?
items.correct: They are receding from us ever faster
items.misconception: They are receding but are slowing down
items.why: Everything a student has seen thrown or fired slows down afterwards, so a universe that started with a bang is expected to be losing speed rather than gaining it. The specification states the opposite: since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster. That is why the observations mattered enough to change the accepted picture.
items.random_wrong: They have stopped receding from us

items.q: Every distant galaxy is observed to be receding, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it recedes. Why is this evidence of an expanding universe?
items.correct: Space itself is stretching, so galaxies separate faster the further apart they are
items.misconception: We are at the centre of the explosion, so everything else moves away from us
items.why: The observation really is that things recede from us in all directions, and the only everyday situation that produces that pattern is standing at the middle of something blowing apart. Because space itself is expanding, an observer in any galaxy would see the same thing: all the other galaxies receding, and the distant ones receding fastest. The observation therefore identifies no centre at all.
items.random_wrong: The galaxies were thrown outwards through space and have never slowed since

items.q: How does the observed red-shift provide evidence for the Big Bang model?
items.correct: Galaxies are separating now, so in the past matter was in a far smaller, denser region
items.misconception: Red-shift proves that the Big Bang happened, so no other model can now be tested
items.why: Students treat strong supporting evidence as final proof, and school science is often presented as a list of settled answers rather than as models held up by evidence. The specification says the red-shift supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations from 1998 onwards show how a theory can be added to when new evidence appears, and dark mass and dark energy show how much is still unexplained.
items.random_wrong: The red glow we detect is the flash of the explosion still on its way to us

items.q: Which statement best describes how scientists were able to use observations to arrive at the Big Bang theory?
items.correct: They observed the red-shift of distant galaxies and built a theory that explains it
items.misconception: They decided what the theory should say, then looked for facts that would fit it
items.why: The everyday word theory means a hunch, and an event long before any observer seems to be beyond the reach of evidence. A scientific theory has to account for observations that can be made now. The red-shift of light from distant galaxies is observed today, and any theory of the universe has to explain it; that is how observations lead to theories.
items.random_wrong: They proved the theory by an experiment, so it can never be altered by anyone

items.q: Which statement about dark mass and dark energy matches the specification?
items.correct: They are examples of what is still not understood about the universe
items.misconception: They are fully explained by the Big Bang theory as it currently stands
items.why: The two ideas are named confidently in textbooks and documentaries, and being named makes them sound settled rather than open. The specification names them precisely as examples of what is not understood. Naming something is not the same as explaining it, and a correct answer must say that these remain unexplained.
items.random_wrong: They are two different names used by scientists for the very same thing

items.q: The pattern of lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy is compared with the pattern produced by the same element in a laboratory. The galaxy's lines are all found closer to the red end. What does this show?
items.correct: The wavelength has increased, so the galaxy is receding from us
items.misconception: The wavelength has decreased, so the galaxy is receding from us
items.why: Students remember that a shift happens but not its direction, and the mental picture of something being stretched or squashed is easy to reverse when the wave diagram is not drawn. Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, so a shift towards the red end must be an increase in wavelength. The specification defines red-shift as an observed increase in wavelength.
items.random_wrong: The wavelength has increased, so the galaxy is approaching us

items.q: Light from galaxies X, Y and Z is examined. X shows a small increase in wavelength, Y a medium increase and Z a large increase. Which galaxy is furthest away, and which is moving fastest?
items.correct: Z is furthest away and Z is moving fastest
items.misconception: X is furthest away and X is moving fastest
items.why: Everyday objects lose speed with distance travelled, so a student applies that pattern and inverts the relationship the specification actually states. The specification states the relationship directly: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Distance and speed increase together.
items.random_wrong: Z is furthest away and X is moving fastest

items.q: The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards changed what scientists say about the expansion of the universe. What does this show about scientific theories?
items.correct: New observations can change what an accepted theory says
items.misconception: Once a theory is accepted new observations cannot alter it
items.why: Students treat strong supporting evidence as final proof, and school science is often presented as a list of settled answers rather than as models held up by evidence. The specification says the red-shift supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations from 1998 onwards show how a theory can be added to when new evidence appears, and dark mass and dark energy show how much is still unexplained.
items.random_wrong: New observations showed the expansion has been slowing down

items.q: Explain qualitatively why light from a galaxy that is receding is observed with a longer wavelength than the same light produced on Earth.
items.correct: The galaxy moves away as the light travels, so the waves reach us stretched out
items.misconception: The light slows down on its long journey, so its waves are longer on arrival
items.why: Students transfer the idea that a moving object loses speed over a long journey to light, and then reach for the wave equation to link a lower speed to a longer wavelength. The observed increase in wavelength is linked to the recession of the galaxy, not to the light tiring on the way. The bigger the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is moving and the further away it is.
items.random_wrong: The light loses energy in dust in space, which reddens it as a sunset is reddened

items.q: A distant galaxy shows a large red-shift. Does that mean the galaxy looks red?
items.correct: No. Red-shift means the wavelength of the light has increased, so features in the spectrum sit closer to the red end than they do in the laboratory.
items.misconception: Red-shift means the galaxy has turned red, so a strongly red-shifted galaxy is a red one and a galaxy that is not red is not red-shifted.
items.why: The name contains a colour, and the only shift a student has met before is a change of colour, so the term is read as a description of appearance rather than of wavelength. The evidence for red-shift is the position of lines in a spectrum, not the overall colour. The whole pattern of lines from a known element is found at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern, and that shift towards the red end is what the word describes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than galaxy A. What does that tell you about B?
items.correct: Galaxy B is further away than galaxy A and is moving faster than galaxy A.
items.misconception: A bigger red-shift means a bigger or brighter galaxy, because a large bright galaxy sends more light and so gives a bigger effect.
items.why: Students associate a larger measured effect with a larger or brighter source, as they do with loudness and with brightness, and transfer that to a shift in wavelength. The size of the red-shift depends on how fast the galaxy is receding and therefore on how far away it is. The size and brightness of the galaxy do not appear in the relationship at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are dark mass and dark energy two names for the same thing?
items.correct: No. They are two separate examples the specification gives of what is still not understood about the universe.
items.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy both mean the invisible stuff out in space, so the two terms can be swapped over freely.
items.why: Both terms begin with dark and both stand for something unseen, so they blur together in memory as one vague idea. The specification lists them separately, as two examples. Mass and energy are different physical quantities and the terms must not be exchanged in an answer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What sort of event does the Big Bang theory describe?
items.correct: It describes the universe beginning from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
items.misconception: The Big Bang was an enormous star that blew up, in the same way that a supernova is a star exploding.
items.why: Supernovae are mentioned in the same short section of the specification, and both ideas involve something violent and bright, so the two are merged into one story. The Big Bang theory is about the beginning of the whole universe from a very small, extremely hot and dense region. Supernovae are separate objects observed since 1998 onwards, whose light tells us how distant galaxies are receding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which observations first led scientists to the Big Bang theory?
items.correct: The observed red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.
items.misconception: The Big Bang theory came from the supernova observations made since 1998 onwards, since those are the observations named with a date.
items.why: The date 1998 is the only date in the section, so it is remembered as the moment the whole theory was worked out. Red-shift is the evidence that the universe is expanding and that supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations came later and added something further: that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A galaxy is observed to be red-shifted. Is it moving towards us or away from us?
items.correct: Away from us. Red-shift is observed in light from galaxies that are receding.
items.misconception: A galaxy coming towards us would push its light waves out in front of it and stretch them, so an increased wavelength means it is approaching.
items.why: The idea of a wave being pushed ahead of a moving source sounds like stretching, and without a clear diagram the direction of the effect is guessed. The specification links the increase in wavelength to galaxies that are receding. The waves are stretched because the source is moving away while the light travels.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Could the red-shift of light from distant galaxies be caused by dust in space?
items.correct: No. The increase in wavelength is evidence that the galaxies are receding and that space itself is expanding.
items.misconception: The light passes through dust on its long journey and loses energy, which reddens it in the way a sunset is reddened.
items.why: Students know that the setting Sun looks red because of the atmosphere, and offer the same explanation for anything described as red. Red-shift is identified by the whole pattern of spectral lines appearing at longer wavelengths, and the size of that shift is larger for the more distant, faster galaxies. That systematic link to distance and speed is what makes it evidence of an expanding universe.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
